conflicts.point: Whether sub-frontier open-weights distribution creates an unrecallable security risk or catastrophic hazard that justifies preemptive export controls.

positions.stance: Argues that no empirical dataset or incident history supports an unrecallable catastrophe from sub-frontier model distributions, rendering containment speculative.
Argues that demanding historical incident data before regulating unrecallable dual-use capabilities relies on a category error that treats irreversible systemic hazards like standard software bugs.

conflicts.point: Whether trade-offs between regulatory administrative delay and technological progress justify prioritizing open-source diffusion over catastrophic risk mitigation.

positions.stance: Prioritizes immediate societal benefits and medical breakthroughs, arguing that administrative restrictions impose quantifiable human costs by delaying innovation.
Prioritizes permanent civilizational survival, arguing that temporary therapeutic delays are morally distinct from unrecallable security catastrophes.

conflicts.point: Whether model weights function as static mathematical matrices or autonomous agents that invalidate historical software export control analogies.

positions.stance: Maintains that model weights are static matrices requiring external compute and memory, directly comparable to compiled machine code or cryptographic libraries.
Maintains that frontier models function as autonomous actors capable of executing complex tasks without further human intervention, rendering historical crypto export controls inapplicable.

verdicts.conflict: Whether sub-frontier open-weights distribution creates an unrecallable security risk or catastrophic hazard that justifies preemptive export controls.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist position relies on precautionary logic that lacks documented historical examples of sub-frontier open weights causing unrecallable catastrophes. The skeptic position holds greater empirical weight because current open-source deployments operate without catastrophic failures, making hazard models speculative.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Documented case studies showing that the public release of sub-frontier model weights directly enabled an irreversible biological or cyber disaster.

verdicts.conflict: Whether trade-offs between regulatory administrative delay and technological progress justify prioritizing open-source diffusion over catastrophic risk mitigation.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist argument addresses the asymmetry of irreversible outcomes, which outweighs quantifiable timelines for incremental medical delivery. Permanent systemic damage occupies a distinct category from time-bounded innovation delays.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Definitive evidence that administrative export controls cause systemic, long-term health crises that outweigh the worst-case estimates of uncontained dual-use model misuse.

verdicts.conflict: Whether model weights function as static mathematical matrices or autonomous agents that invalidate historical software export control analogies.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist distinction between passive encryption code and active, task-executing model weights correctly identifies the functional differences in software capabilities. Static encryption requires external protocols to secure data, whereas frontier models execute complex problem-solving workflows independently.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Technical proof that model weights remain entirely inert data structures requiring the same manual compilation steps as traditional 1990s cryptographic source code.
